slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study The Proposal, a one-act comedy by the Russian writer Anton Chekhov, in which a marriage proposal keeps collapsing into ridiculous quarrels. Please read the play itself in your textbook, First Flight. This lesson does not repeat its dialogue. Instead we will follow the action, understand the characters, and see how Chekhov makes us laugh at pride and greed.

slides.heading: How to study a play
bullets: Read the play once in *First Flight*; if you can, read it aloud with friends, one part each.
Notice the **stage directions** as well as the dialogue: they show feelings and actions.
In answers, **report** what characters say in your own words; never quote lines.
Practise the extract questions, which use SOYL commentary on key exchanges.
slides.narration: A play is written to be performed, so study it a little differently. Read it in your textbook, and if possible read it aloud with friends. Pay attention to the stage directions, which show how characters feel and move. In answers, report what characters say in your own words instead of quoting them. Then practise with our extract questions on key exchanges.

slides.narration: Anton Chekhov lived from eighteen sixty to nineteen oh four. He trained as a doctor and became one of Russia's greatest writers of plays and short stories. The Proposal is a one-act farce, a fast comedy built on exaggeration. It is set in the drawing room of a country house in nineteenth-century Russia, and we read it in English translation.

slides.narration: There are only three characters. Chubukov is a landowner, and Natalya is his daughter. Lomov is their neighbour, also a landowner, and very nervous about his health. Two dogs are mentioned, Lomov's dog Guess and the Chubukovs' dog Squeezer, and they matter more than you might expect. Learn the names well, because answers must say clearly who does what.

visual.caption: The play in six movements (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The play moves in six steps. Lomov arrives to propose. Alone, he explains to himself why he must marry. He and Natalya quarrel over the Oxen Meadows. He leaves, and the truth comes out. Brought back, he quarrels again, this time about dogs. He collapses, revives, and is engaged, and the quarrelling starts again. Keep this map in mind.

slides.heading: Summary 1: the arrival and the request
slides.body_md: Lomov arrives at Chubukov's house dressed formally. Chubukov welcomes him warmly but, in an aside to the audience, suspects he wants a loan. Nervously, Lomov explains that he has come to ask for Natalya's hand. Chubukov is delighted, embraces him and goes to call his daughter. Alone, Lomov reasons that he is at an age to marry and needs an orderly life, while worrying aloud about his health.
slides.narration: Lomov arrives in formal clothes. Chubukov greets him warmly, though privately he suspects his neighbour wants money. Nervously, Lomov explains that he wants to marry Natalya. Chubukov is delighted and goes to fetch her. Left alone, Lomov reasons that it is time to marry and that he needs a calm, orderly life. He never mentions love, but he mentions his heart many times.

slides.heading: Summary 2: the first quarrel
slides.body_md: Natalya enters, not knowing why Lomov has come. Leading up to his proposal, he recalls the families' long friendship and refers to the Oxen Meadows as his. Natalya insists the Meadows belong to her family. The argument grows heated, and Chubukov returns and sides with his daughter. Threats of court action and insults about each other's relatives follow, and Lomov leaves, clutching his heart.
slides.narration: Natalya comes in, with no idea why Lomov is there. He takes the long road to his proposal, recalling the families' friendship, and calls the Oxen Meadows his. Natalya says they belong to her family. Neither gives way. Chubukov joins in on his daughter's side, and soon there are threats of court and insults about relatives. Lomov staggers out.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events of the play are shuffled. Put them in the order in which they happen, from Lomov's arrival to the engagement.

slides.heading: Summary 3: the truth comes out
slides.body_md: After Lomov leaves, Chubukov lets slip that he had come to propose. Natalya becomes hysterical and demands that he be brought back. Chubukov fetches him, and Natalya, now all sweetness, concedes that the Meadows are his.
slides.narration: Once Lomov has gone, Chubukov reveals that he had come to propose. Natalya's anger turns instantly to despair, and she demands that her father bring him back. When Lomov returns, she is gentle and gives way about the Meadows. For a moment, it seems the proposal can finally be made. But Chekhov has another quarrel waiting.

slides.heading: Summary 4: the dogs, the collapse and the engagement
slides.body_md: Talk turns to hunting. Lomov praises his dog Guess; Natalya insists her family's Squeezer is better, and Lomov finds fault with Squeezer's jaw. Chubukov joins in, and the quarrel grows until Lomov collapses into a chair. Thinking him dead, the others panic. When he revives, Chubukov hurries the couple into an engagement, but they start arguing about the dogs again, and Chubukov calls for champagne.
slides.narration: Then the talk turns to hunting dogs. Lomov praises his dog Guess, and Natalya insists that Squeezer is better. Chubukov joins in, and the quarrel grows until Lomov collapses. The others think he is dead. When he revives, Chubukov rushes them into an engagement. Within moments they are arguing about the dogs again, and Chubukov calls for champagne.

slides.heading: Theme 1: a marriage of convenience
slides.body_md: Chekhov mocks marriage treated as a practical bargain.
columns:
**What drives the match**

- Lomov feels it is time to marry
- he wants an orderly life
- Chubukov wants his daughter settled with a neighbour of property
- Natalya is eager not to lose a suitor

**What is missing**

- any word of love
- patience or tenderness
- willingness to give way
- harmony, even at the engagement
slides.narration: The first theme is the marriage of convenience. Lomov wants a wife because it is time and he needs an orderly life. Chubukov wants his daughter settled with a neighbour who owns land. Natalya does not want to lose a suitor. What is missing? Love, tenderness, and any willingness to give way. Chekhov makes us laugh, but the criticism is serious.

Hypocrisy, in Chubukov's warm welcome and private suspicion. And materialism, because property shapes every relationship. In long answers, link two or three of these themes with clear evidence.

slides.narration: Let us sketch the characters. Lomov is nervous and a hypochondriac, yet stubborn and easily provoked. Natalya is proud, sharp-tongued and possessive, but desperate to marry. Chubukov is hypocritical, hot-tempered and eager to see his daughter married. None of them will give way, and that is exactly what makes the comedy work.

slides.heading: Two quarrels, one pattern
columns:
**What repeats**

- a claim, a counter-claim, rising anger
- Chubukov joining in
- Lomov's heart troubles getting worse

**What changes**

- the subject grows even more trivial
- the second quarrel ends in a collapse
- the engagement is made, yet the quarrel goes on

visual.caption: The same pattern, an even smaller cause (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Compare the two quarrels. The pattern repeats: a claim, a counter-claim, rising anger, Chubukov joining in, and Lomov's heart getting worse. What changes is the subject, which becomes even sillier, moving from land to dogs. The second quarrel ends in a collapse and an engagement, but the arguing goes on. Repetition is one of Chekhov's main comic tools.

slides.heading: Technique 1: farce
bullets: **Exaggeration:** a proposal swallowed by disputes over a meadow and two dogs.
**Extreme mood swings:** affection to fury, fury to tears.
**Physical comedy:** clutching the chest, staggering out, collapsing as if dead.
**Fast pace and repetition:** two quarrels on the same pattern, a third beginning at the end.
**Satire:** laughter that exposes greed, pride and pettiness.
slides.narration: Why is the play a farce? It exaggerates, letting a proposal be swallowed by fights over a meadow and dogs. Moods swing wildly. There is physical comedy, from clutching the chest to collapsing as if dead. The pace is fast, and the quarrels repeat. All of this makes us laugh, and through laughter Chekhov mocks greed, pride and pettiness.

slides.heading: Technique 2: irony and stage directions
bullets: **Stage directions** tell actors how to move and speak; they reveal nerves, anger, tears and collapse.
**Asides** let the audience hear a character's private thoughts.

slides.narration: Irony runs through the play. The situation is ironic, because a proposal becomes a quarrel. There is dramatic irony, because Natalya fights Lomov without knowing why he came. And an aside reveals the gap between Chubukov's warm words and his suspicion. Stage directions matter too: they show nervousness, anger, tears and the collapse, which the dialogue alone cannot show.

slides.heading: Asides and stage directions: SOYL's own scene
slides.body_md: A tiny scene written by SOYL (not from the play) to show how the devices work. A shopkeeper greets a customer:
bullets: *Stage direction:* the shopkeeper bows low and rubs his hands together.
*Spoken aloud:* the shopkeeper says how honoured he is by such a fine visitor.
*Aside:* he mutters to the audience that the man still owes him for last month.
*Effect:* the audience sees the gap between his words and his thoughts, which is the source of the comedy.
slides.narration: Here is a tiny scene of our own. A stage direction tells us the shopkeeper bows and rubs his hands. Aloud, he says he is honoured by his fine visitor. In an aside, he tells the audience the man still owes him money. The gap between words and thoughts makes us laugh. Now look for the same device when Chubukov welcomes Lomov in your textbook.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the play. A farce is a comedy of exaggeration, and satire mocks human folly. An aside is a remark to the audience. A stage direction tells actors what to do. A hypochondriac is always anxious about imagined illness, and palpitations are a racing heartbeat. Convenience means what is practical or advantageous.

sections.heading: 1. About the play and the author
sections.body_md:
**Read the play itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the play's dialogue or stage directions.

**Anton Chekhov** (1860–1904) was a Russian dramatist and short-story writer who trained as a doctor. *The Proposal* is a **one-act farce** set in the drawing room of Chubukov's country house in nineteenth-century Russia, read in English translation. Its three characters are **Chubukov**, a landowner; **Natalya**, his daughter; and **Lomov**, a nervous neighbouring landowner.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**The request.** Lomov arrives formally dressed. Chubukov welcomes him while privately suspecting he wants a loan. Lomov asks for Natalya's hand; Chubukov is delighted and fetches her. Alone, Lomov reasons that it is time to marry and that he needs an orderly life, worrying aloud about his health.

**Quarrel 1.** Natalya, unaware of the proposal, disputes Lomov's claim to the Oxen Meadows. Chubukov joins in on her side; threats and insults about relatives follow; Lomov leaves, clutching his heart.

**The truth.** Chubukov reveals that Lomov had come to propose. Natalya becomes hysterical and demands his return. When he comes back she concedes the Meadows.

**Quarrel 2.** Talk of hunting leads to a dispute over whose dog is better, Lomov's Guess or the Chubukovs' Squeezer. Chubukov joins in; Lomov collapses and is thought dead.

**The ending.** Lomov revives; Chubukov hurries the couple into an engagement; they resume arguing about the dogs; Chubukov calls for champagne.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Marriage of convenience:** practical reasons, no mention of love.
- **Pride and possessiveness:** fights over land and dogs.
- **Quarrelsome human nature:** two quarrels, and a third at the engagement.
- **Hypocrisy:** Chubukov's warm welcome and private suspicion.
- **Materialism:** property shapes every relationship.

**Message:** pride and greed make people quarrel over trifles, even at moments that should be joyful; marriage built on convenience promises little harmony.

sections.heading: 4. Characters
sections.body_md:
**Lomov:** nervous (stammers his request), a hypochondriac (always worrying about his heart), practical about marriage, yet stubborn and easily provoked (will not yield on land or dogs; threatens court; collapses).

**Natalya:** proud and sharp-tongued (defends the Meadows and Squeezer), possessive, eager to marry (hysterics on learning of the proposal), changeable (concedes the Meadows, then fights about dogs).

**Chubukov:** hypocritical (warm words, private suspicion), hot-tempered (joins both quarrels with insults), eager to marry off his daughter (rushes the engagement).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5), short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) and long answers (6 marks, 100–120 words) from *First Flight* (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events and speeches, accurately reported), interpretation (a clear, supported view), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Swapping the dogs: Guess is Lomov's, Squeezer is the Chubukovs'.
2. Saying Natalya knew of the proposal during the first quarrel: she learns of it only after Lomov leaves.
3. Forgetting that Natalya concedes the Meadows before the dog quarrel.
4. Calling the play a tragedy or a romance: it is a farce.
5. Quoting dialogue from memory instead of reporting it in your own words.

**Remember:** read the play in your textbook, *First Flight*.

questions.stem_md: *The Proposal* is a satire on marriages of convenience and on quarrelsome human nature. Discuss, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Marriage of convenience (Lomov’s reasons; Chubukov’s eagerness; Natalya’s desperation) + quarrelsomeness (Meadows, dogs, insults, the ending) + how exaggeration creates satire. Conclude.

answer.model_answer_md: Chekhov shows marriage treated as a practical bargain. Lomov wants a wife because he thinks he has reached the right age and needs a calm, orderly life; love is never mentioned. Chubukov is eager to settle his daughter with a neighbour of property, and Natalya, though she quarrels fiercely, is desperate not to lose a suitor. At the same time, all three are absurdly quarrelsome. A proposal dissolves into fights about a meadow and then about two dogs, with insults about relatives thrown in. Even the engagement is drowned in argument. By exaggerating these traits, Chekhov makes us laugh at greed, pride and pettiness, and at marriages built on convenience rather than affection.

answer.model_answer_md: Lomov is a nervous, anxious man. He arrives in formal dress and stammers before he can explain his purpose. He is a hypochondriac, forever worrying about his heart and his sleep, and he finally collapses as if dead. His reasons for marrying are practical, not romantic: he feels the time has come and wants an orderly life. Despite his nerves, he is stubborn and quarrelsome, refusing to yield over the Oxen Meadows and insisting that Guess is better than Squeezer. He is also easily provoked, threatening to go to court. Lomov is a comic figure whose pride and anxiety keep defeating his own purpose, so that even his proposal is almost lost in quarrels.

questions.stem_md: How does Chekhov use the elements of farce to create humour in *The Proposal*? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Features of farce with examples: exaggeration (trivial disputes), extreme mood swings, physical comedy (Lomov’s collapse), irony, pace and repetition. Conclude with the overall effect.

answer.model_answer_md: Chekhov builds the play on exaggeration. A simple proposal becomes a battle, first over a meadow of little value and then over which dog is better. The characters swing between extremes: Chubukov from affection to insults, Natalya from fury to tears and back again. Physical comedy adds to the fun. Lomov clutches his heart, complains of numbness and finally collapses, and the others panic over his apparent death. Irony runs throughout, since the audience knows of the proposal while Natalya does not, and the engagement is celebrated amid shouting. Rapid exchanges and repeated quarrels keep the pace frantic. Every element pushes ordinary behaviour to absurd lengths, which is the essence of farce.

questions.solution_md: Types of irony with examples: situational (proposal becomes quarrel; celebration amid argument), dramatic (Natalya’s ignorance), the aside revealing hypocrisy. Conclude on what irony exposes.

answer.model_answer_md: Irony is at the heart of the play’s humour. The central situation is ironic: Lomov comes to propose to Natalya, yet spends most of his visit fighting with her. Dramatic irony adds to this, because the audience knows his purpose while Natalya does not, so we watch her ruin her own chances without realising it. Chubukov’s warm welcome hides his private suspicion that Lomov wants a loan, an irony revealed through his aside. The ending is the sharpest irony of all. A couple who have just agreed to marry are already arguing about dogs, while Chubukov calls for champagne to celebrate the match. Through irony, Chekhov exposes the gap between appearance and reality.

questions.stem_md: Are the follies Chekhov mocks in *The Proposal* still found today? Answer in 100–120 words, with reference to the play.

answer.model_answer_md: Many of the follies Chekhov mocks are still with us. Marriages are sometimes arranged mainly around property, income or social status, much as Lomov’s choice rests on practical convenience and Chubukov’s on a suitable neighbour. People still quarrel bitterly over small things. Neighbours fight over boundary walls, relatives over inherited land, and friends over which team or brand is better, just as Lomov and Natalya fight over a meadow and two dogs. Pride makes such disputes hard to end. Social media can even magnify them. The play remains funny because we recognise ourselves in it. Its lesson is timeless: pride and possessiveness can spoil even the happiest occasions.
